profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab about why a follow-up reproduction of the paper "Blind Descent: A Prequel to Gradient Descent" is no longer matching the paper's proof-of-concept CNN behavior after the codebase was consolidated for a new internal benchmark suite. Context: the team expected the Blind Descent CNN on CIFAR-10 to at least recover the modest learning signal reported in the paper, but recent runs either flatten early or vary wildly across seeds. Agenda: compare what each person thinks the failing symptom is, identify whether the issue is coming from code drift, randomness handling, or evaluation setup, and decide on one concrete rerun plan for the afternoon. Expected outcome: they leave believing they have agreed on the root-cause hypothesis and on a 'same setup' verification run, even though some assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Leena Voss
members.role: Postdoctoral researcher and first author of the Blind Descent paper
members.expertise: optimization theory, experimental design for alternative learning rules, small-scale proof-of-concept neural network studies
members.background: Leena developed the original Blind Descent formulation during her PhD and wrote most of the archived research code used for the camera-ready experiments; she now supervises follow-up replications but no longer runs the day-to-day infrastructure herself.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the paper's core claim that Blind Descent can genuinely learn without gradients, and she is worried that recent failures might actually be due to silent implementation drift rather than a flaw in the idea; she also wants a quick diagnosis that does not reopen the whole experimental story.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the paper setup,' they mean the archived camera-ready branch tagged before submission, not later cleanup merges that seemed mathematically harmless.
For Blind Descent, the perturbation-direction random stream is part of the effective initialization because it shapes the whole search trajectory from step one.
An 'instability' problem mainly means optimization dynamics stop making progress or become erratic during training, even if some seeds eventually land on decent accuracy.
A 'CIFAR sanity check' still uses the full training split and normal paper-length training; it is just a lighter reporting standard, not a smaller data slice.

members.name: Arun Patel
members.role: Research engineer supporting reproducibility and benchmarking
members.expertise: PyTorch training pipelines, experiment tracking, reproducibility tooling, refactoring research code into maintainable benchmark suites
members.background: Arun joined the lab after the paper was accepted and rebuilt the original experiments into the lab's shared training framework, adding deterministic data loaders, branch cleanup, and a layerwise perturbation normalization option that he regards as a non-substantive implementation fix.
members.private_state: He wants to show that the integrated benchmark pipeline is reliable and that any remaining issue is due to known variance in the method, not because his refactor changed the experiment in a meaningful way; he also wants a fast diagnostic run that fits into available GPU time.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the paper setup,' they mean the current maintained implementation that preserves the intended algorithm, including cleanup patches merged after submission.
Initialization refers to the initial network weights; the perturbation samples drawn during training are ordinary run-time randomness and do not count as part of 'same init.'
An 'instability' problem mainly means poor reproducibility across seeds at the endpoint, since occasional flat runs are expected for a stochastic search method.
A 'sanity check on CIFAR' means the lab's standard 10k debug shard with production transforms and a short run, because full-length CIFAR jobs are reserved for confirmation once plumbing is verified.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to rerunning 'the paper CNN setup' or 'the original setup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the archived camera-ready code path on the old branch, before later cleanup merges such as layerwise perturbation normalization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the current benchmark-suite implementation on main, which he believes is the same setup in cleaned-up form and therefore still 'the paper setup.'
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one paper and one intended CNN experiment in their shared memory, so the phrase feels uniquely identifying; the later patch was treated as housekeeping, making neither person expect that 'paper setup' could point to different code.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to rerun with 'the same initialization' to see whether the failure reproduces.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means matching both the starting weights and the fixed perturbation-direction RNG table used by the original Blind Descent run, because both determine the search path.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means reusing the same weight initialization seed while allowing the perturbation sampler to draw a fresh sequence, since he treats those samples as ordinary stochasticity after initialization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In standard deep-learning practice, 'initialization' almost always refers only to weights, so the surface phrase feels obvious; Blind Descent's dependence on perturbation trajectories is unusual enough that neither realizes the other is using a different procedural convention.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the current issue is 'instability' and discuss checking whether the run is stable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the training dynamics flatten or oscillate too early, so Blind Descent is failing to keep making progress after the first dozen epochs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the final results vary too much across nominally identical seeds, even though some runs still show progress and reach acceptable loss curves.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both symptoms plausibly belong under the everyday label 'instability,' and in a troubleshooting conversation it is natural to move fluidly between them without explicitly defining the term.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a 'CIFAR sanity check'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both propose a 'quick CIFAR sanity check' before doing anything bigger.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the full CIFAR-10 training split with the paper's train/val handling and a near-full training horizon, just without a full ablation sweep.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the lab's standard 10k debug shard for 20 epochs with the same transforms, used only to verify that the refactored pipeline is behaving sensibly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'sanity check' is intentionally informal and lab-local, so it sounds aligned while hiding different assumptions about the boundary between a debug run and a substantive reproduction.

What worries me is the curve shape: in the camera-ready branch the CNN at least kept inching downward for a while, whereas now it sounds like progress dies almost immediately. If this is just implementation drift after the archived version, we can diagnose it quickly.
